content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper reconstructs high-frequency information (individual spikes) from low pass filtered neural recordings using a deep learning based reconstruction algorithm. They present a transformer based architecture and a sampling approach to learn this model. The authors show that this approach works by magnifying a little bit of high frequency information causal low pass filters, but the approach does not work with ideal filter.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper presents work on an important problem in neural engineering. The empirical evaluation seems reasonable and complete. However, some improvements can be made in my opinion:

1. Present quantitative evaluation across multiple channels of some of the observations: such as delay and amplitude differences in Figure 3, clustering performance in Figure 5. 

2. How representative is the performance for realistic recordings? The main shortcoming of this paper might be that it might not be noticed by most people in neuroengineering since it is not clear how the results would translate to different neural recordings. 

A figure indicating performance metric vs SNR might be useful. You can add artificial noise in various frequency bands and see how the algorithm performs.  This way, I can look at the range of SNR in a new set of recordings (different brain region, etc) and asses the potential impact of this approach.

3. In a similar vein, how much is the accuracy when you apply the pipeline end to end? If you take the predicted spikes, and find threshold crossings, spike clustering and waveform estimation without using ground truth, how much is the final performance? What is the false positivity rate of detecting spikes? Again, having this might really help improving the impact of the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is quite clear. The analyses seem well done.
content.summary_of_the_review:
More empirical analysis as suggested above should improve the impact on neural engineering community.  It is a very interesting idea, but after reading the paper, I am not convinced that this approach will help me with my data - and more the suggestions above might help with that. 

I would be happy to increase the score if some effort is made in this direction.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The present study did comprehensive simulations to show the reconstruction of high-frequency spiking information from downsampled neuronal signals from in vitro and in vivo neural data. The only weakness I can tell is the clarity of writing.

### Writing
- Please explain the full name of abbreviations when they first appear. For example, I am confused about what Ours-D and Ours mean at the bottom of page 1.

- Eqs. 6-7: $f_\theta$ and $g_\phi$ are undefined and not explained at all. And it is unclear about what the parameter set $\theta$ and $\phi$ are.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this manuscript, the authors describe a method for extrapolating the high-frequency content of extracellular spike recordings from low-pass-filtered and highly-subsampled data. This configuration is meant to simulate recording spikes at radically reduced sampling rates on the order of 1-5 kHz, rather than the more typical >25kHz. The described technique involves the use of a Swin transformer, Fourier interpolation, and jittering spike locations within training batches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

1. Extrapolating spike waveforms from low-sampling-rate data is a potentially impactful area. If one could record spikes at 1 kHz, e.g., this could be transformative from brain-machine-interfaces and wireless recording.
2. The use of a Swin transformer in this problem domain is novel.
3. At face value the results appear impressive.

**Weaknesses**

1. Non-triviality of the result. Since the spikes used throughout the manuscript appear to have a fair amount of frequency content <1kHz, especially in the MEA dataset where things look the best, it is unclear what the network is adding exactly and whether it is non-trivial.
	1. In figures 3 and 4 the spike locations are clearly visible in the low-passed signal. Simple controls are missing. For instance, what if spike detection is attempted on the raw low-passed signal? What’s the hit rate if you simply take the derivative of the low-passed signal and then square the result? What if you high-pass it? What if you use linear methods rather than deep learning (e.g. LMS filters)?
	2. Same question in Figure 5. How does the feature space look if you simply use the low-passed data (e.g. just do a simple high-pass on the traces prior to being fed into the Swin transformer)? What is being added by the network? 
	3. Most of the results focus on the MEA dataset, where spikes are high SNR and appear to have low-frequency structure. Does the model perform worse on the in vivo datasets because the spikes are higher frequency and lower SNR (especially in the HIPPO dataset)? This would imply that the model will not generalize to common settings.
	4. On a related note, why were the baseline models not included after Figure 4?
2. Model generality. Ideally, the model would learn to extrapolate any high-frequency spike shape from its low-pass filtered versions. If this were true, the model would perform well on datasets where the high-frequency spike shapes diverged from those in the training set. Based on the presented results, this does not seem to be the case.
	1. The clearest demonstration of this is training on MEA1 and testing on HIPPO. Broadly speaking, if the quality of the reconstruction strongly depends on how closely the reconstructed signal matches what the model was trained on, then the model is not effectively generalizing. The authors would need to demonstrate that the quality of reconstruction is not simply a function of how similar the high-frequency spikes are to what’s contained in the training dataset.
	2. It is also unclear how strongly this would depend on the anti-aliasing filter used. Presumably a lot of what’s left in the low-passed filtered trace is due to: (1) any frequency content in the spike <1 kHz and (2) the specific characteristics of the anti-aliasing filter (e.g. impulse response, group delay, etc.). Do the authors imagine that the model can generalize to variability in the anti-aliasing filter itself?

minor issues


1. Anti-aliasing filter is zero-phase digital here. In practice an anti-aliasing filter in hardware would be analog. Comment on why the choice of “anti-aliasing” filter was a good simulation of what one would use in hardware.
2. A related point here is the authors refer to aliasing through the manuscript. Do they think information results from genuine signal *aliasing* or simply that the non-ideal filter has a gradual rolloff and thus preserves a fair amount of information between 200 Hz and Nyquist at each subsampled rate (e.g. 200-500 Hz for the x25 subsample)?  
3. The hardware filters used for acquiring data. In the MEA dataset the firmware filter was 3.5 kHz. If signals were low-passed at 3.5 kHz, then high-frequency information is actually excluded from all analysis. Presumably this would make reconstruction simpler, since you don’t have as many fine time-scale features to reconstruct. Same question for the in vivo data (7.6 kHz). Can the authors comment on this?
4. How robust is the model to noise? If you add noise, or insert impulses into the low-passed data prior to extrapolation, what does the model produce? I am concerned that the model may create spikes where none exist in high noise settings.
5. In Table 1 model performance for all models seems better on MEA2 *even though the training set was MEA1,* which is surprising.  This could be true, but I just want to be sure this isn't a typo.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I found the manuscript generally clear. 

The Swin transformer itself is based on previously published work, though the authors apply it in a novel setting – reconstructing high-frequency spikes from low-frequency data. The use of jittering during training is a good idea, though I would say not a huge advance in of itself.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the idea presented in the paper is not necessarily a bad one, the lack of proper controls leaves open the possibility that many of the results are fairly trivial. Additionally, it is hard to determine what is driving performance here since the results were not systematically investigated.  See strengths and weaknesses for more details.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This is a straightforward application paper, where the authors use training of a transformer network to reconstruct high frequency multi-electrode array recordings (data collected both in vivo and in vitro)  from corresponding lowpassed then subsampled signal. The authors found good reconstruction results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: Novelty of the paper is the application of transformer networks to (the last few years have seen their application to all sorts of domains) reconstruct multi-electrode array data.
Weakness: There is little we can say beyond, here is another paper where we apply transformers to a particular dataset. Also, this reviewer suspects that the trained network might fail when handed new MEA data from a different animal subject. MEA data is highly personalized. It depends on the nuances of the location of the MEA recording protocols and varoius other things. In order to really trust this technique, the authors need to apply the trained network to a "completely different"  recording. Not a train test protocol where data is selected from the same recording.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Very clearly written. The reviewer believes that the results can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: At a high level this paper is a member of the class "transformers applied to dataset X" of papers, which we have seen many of. That in itself does not doom the paper. If the results were trustable, this would indeed lead to efficiencies in the MEA recording field. What makes me suspect the quality of the results is that the model was trained and tested to datasets that were drawn from specific recordings. The usefulness of the results depend on whether the trained transformer can now be used to reconstruct an entirely different recording. That is one where the subject animal is different, the MEA placement is different. In essence, a totally different recording on a different animal. I suspect the good numbers the authors see is a result of the peculiarities of the extra-cellular space that leave a very specific trace of a spike in its lowpassed signal, something that will change from recording to recording.

content.title: Deep High-Frequency Extrapolation for Neuronal Spike Restoration
content.TL;DR: Transformer reconstruction of high-frequency and high-resolution spikes from low-passed neuronal signals
content.abstract: Recording neuronal activity using multiple electrodes has been widely used for studying functional mechanisms of the brain. However, handling massive amounts of data is still a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel strategy to restore high-frequency neuronal spikes from small-volume and low-frequency band signals. Inspired by the fact that high-frequency extrapolation is equivalent to super-resolution problems in 2D signals, we applied a Swin transformer to extrapolate high-frequency information from downsampled neuronal signals both in vitro and in vivo. We found that aliasing components of input signals and the spike jittering-based selection of the training batch improved the performance of reconstructing accurate neuronal spikes. As a result, we observed reasonably restored neuronal spiking activity, including the spike timing, waveforms, and network connectivity, even with the $\times 8$ subsampled dataset.
